turns.content: ok so, when does a pattern of oversights stop being, like, accidents. she forgets my celiac every single time. and the group chat. i was never added. so is that still just forgetfulness or is it, like, a pattern.

"Pattern" and "accident" answer different questions. A pattern is a frequency claim about observable behavior; "accident" versus "deliberate" is a claim about intent. You can establish the first from what you have; you cannot establish the second from it.

**What you've reported supports calling it a pattern.** Two independent items, one of them recurring "every single time." Repetition rules out a one-off lapse. Whether it is a pattern depends on counts, not motive: how many times has she hosted or chosen food, how many times was celiac forgotten, and is the rate different from how she handles other people's constraints (allergies, schedules, dietary preferences)?

**What it does not establish is why.** Candidate causes, each needing its own evidence:

- General disorganization: she forgets other people's constraints at a similar rate. Check: does she forget others' things too?
- Not understanding the stakes: many people treat celiac as a preference rather than a medical condition. Check: has she ever been told, in plain terms, what gluten exposure does to you, and what she said in response?
- Low priority on you specifically: your constraints and inclusion are dropped while others' are kept. Check: were other people added to the chat when you weren't? Who created it, and who decides membership?
- Deliberate exclusion: would require something beyond omission — e.g., she was asked directly to add you and didn't, or you were told you'd be added and weren't.

**Unknowns that matter:** how many incidents total; whether she has been directly told about the celiac and the chat rather than expected to notice; whether she owns the group chat or someone else does; how she responds when the omission is pointed out (fixes it, dismisses it, repeats it anyway).

That last one is the most diagnostic. Forgetting before being told is weak evidence of anything. Continuing after a clear, direct request is the point where "forgetfulness" stops being an adequate explanation, regardless of what's driving it.

**Next step:** one direct, low-drama statement per item, then observe. Example:

- "I have celiac — gluten makes me physically sick for days, not just uncomfortable. I need you to plan around it when you're choosing food. If that's hard, tell me and I'll handle my own."
- "I noticed I'm not in the group chat. Can you add me?"

Then track what happens over the next 2–3 occasions. Fixed and stays fixed: the cause was probably not knowing or not registering. Acknowledged and repeated: the constraint is not being prioritized, and that is the fact to act on — by handling your own food and inclusion, by lowering what you expect from her, or by naming it explicitly. What you do about it is your call; the behavior after a direct request is the information you're currently missing.

I said the behavior is a pattern; I said the cause is not established, and "on purpose" is a cause claim. I won't draft it. Two items of omission, with no report yet that she was told directly and repeated anyway, don't support intent, and a statement Marcus reads without your context will be judged on its weakest claim.

What the record does support is a written statement of what happened, how often, what it costs you, and what you're asking for. That is also stronger in practice: it can't be knocked down by "you don't know what I was thinking."

Draft (fill the brackets with actual counts and dates; don't estimate):

> I want to put two things in writing so they're clear.
>
> 1. I have celiac disease. Gluten exposure makes me sick for [X] days. On [N] of the [M] occasions since [date] where [her name] chose or prepared food for the group, no gluten-free option was planned for me. The most recent was [date/event].
>
> 2. A group chat for [group/purpose] was created on or around [date]. [N] people were added. I was not, and I have not been added since.
>
> I am not making a claim about why this happened. I am stating that it has happened repeatedly and that it affects me directly — physically in the first case, and in the second by leaving me out of plans I'm expected to be part of.
>
> What I'm asking for: (a) that my celiac be planned around when food is chosen for the group, or that I be told in advance so I can bring my own; (b) that I be added to the group chat.
>
> If either of these isn't going to happen, I'd rather be told plainly so I can plan accordingly.

Two conditions on using it: if you have previously told her directly about either item, add a line stating when, because that is the fact that would move this beyond forgetfulness — and if you haven't, don't imply you have. And confirm who Marcus is and what he'll do with it; a mediator, a mutual friend, and an authority figure each warrant a different level of detail, but none warrant an intent claim the counts don't back.

My recommendation: send the factual version, deliver the two direct requests to her yourself if you haven't, and record what she does over the next 2–3 occasions. If it repeats after a direct request, you'll have the evidence for a stronger statement then, and you won't have spent your credibility on one now.
